title: Milestone: Colonies to a House Divided
objective: After this level you can connect colonial slavery, the founders' compromises and westward expansion to explain why the nation split by 1860.
summary: Lincoln’s 1858 House Divided speech names the chapter’s problem: a nation half slave and half free. Removal, cotton, resistance, reform and expansion all fed the split.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway through US history. Why was the nation coming apart?
cards.body: From the Trail of Tears to Bleeding Kansas, this chapter kept circling one question: would slavery spread west? Put it all together.

cards.headline: A house divided
cards.body: On June 16, 1858, in Springfield, Illinois, Abraham Lincoln put the chapter’s problem in one sentence: "A house divided against itself cannot stand." He added: "I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free." Cotton had made slavery more profitable, and each new territory reopened the question the compromises had tried to settle.

cards.headline: Milestone: a house divided
learned: Why cotton, new land and failed compromises left the nation half slave and half free by 1858.
How the Cherokee won in the Supreme Court and still lost their homeland.
How enslaved people resisted, escaped and built families, faith and music of their own.
What abolitionists and Seneca Falls demanded, and why many Americans pushed back.

questions.prompt: A House Divided: which of these came first?

options.label: The Kansas-Nebraska Act
options.rationale: That came in 1854.

options.label: The Compromise of 1850
options.rationale: That came 30 years after Missouri.

options.label: Lincoln’s House Divided speech
options.rationale: That was 1858, the latest of all.

questions.explanation: 1820 Missouri Compromise, then 1850, then 1854, then Lincoln’s 1858 speech.

questions.prompt: Before removal, what had the Cherokee Nation built?

options.label: A written constitution and a newspaper
A canal to the Great Lakes
options.rationale: That was the Erie Canal.

options.label: A confederacy of the Five Nations
options.rationale: That describes the Haudenosaunee.

options.label: Mills that hired farm women
options.rationale: That was Lowell.

questions.explanation: A syllabary (1821), a constitution (1827) and the Cherokee Phoenix (1828).

questions.prompt: About how many trips did Harriet Tubman make back into Maryland to rescue others?

options.label: About 19
options.rationale: That’s the inflated 1868 count.

options.label: About 50
options.rationale: Far more than the record shows.

options.label: About 300
options.rationale: That’s the inflated count of people.

questions.explanation: About 13; the 1868 figure of 19 trips was inflated.

questions.prompt: What problem did Eli Whitney’s cotton gin solve?

options.label: Cotton rotting in the fields in wet weather
options.rationale: The problem was seeds.

options.label: Shipping cotton cheaply to mills in England
options.rationale: The gin cleaned cotton; it didn’t ship it.

options.label: Pulling sticky seeds out of inland cotton
Planting cotton seed in straight rows faster
options.rationale: Planting and picking still took people.

questions.explanation: Inland cotton’s sticky seeds were slow to pick out; the gin pulled the fiber away from them.

questions.prompt: At Seneca Falls, which demand split the delegates?

options.label: Ending the Fugitive Slave Act
options.rationale: That law came two years later.

options.label: Admitting California
options.rationale: That was a Compromise of 1850 question.

options.label: Equal wages in the Lowell mills
options.rationale: Not part of the resolutions here.

questions.explanation: The resolution for the elective franchise was the only one not passed unanimously.

questions.prompt: Lincoln warned in 1858 that the nation could not stay half slave and half free. Which 1854 law had just reopened slavery in territories closed to it since 1820?

options.label: The Indian Removal Act
options.rationale: That was 1830 and about Native lands.

options.label: The Fugitive Slave Act
options.rationale: That was part of 1850.

options.label: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
options.rationale: That 1848 treaty ended the Mexican War.

questions.explanation: Kansas-Nebraska let settlers decide, repealing the Missouri Compromise line.

questions.prompt: How did the war with Mexico lead to the Compromise of 1850?

options.label: It ended the argument over slavery for a generation
options.rationale: It reopened the argument.

options.label: It forced the Cherokee west to Indian Territory
options.rationale: Cherokee removal came in 1838.

options.label: It banned slavery in every state formed from Mexico
options.rationale: New Mexico and Utah could decide for themselves.

options.label: It won new land, reopening the question of slavery there

questions.explanation: Land from Mexico, including California, reopened slave or free, and 1850’s package tried to answer it.
